newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe land law seen eroding investment drive.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe land law seen eroding investment drive.

text.p: Zimbabwe has pumped up its campaign for vital investment, but political and economic analysts said on Wednesday plans by the government to bar foreigners and companies from owning agricultural land may undermine its drive.

President Robert Mugabe told parliament on Tuesday that he would, in the coming year, expand a controversial land acquisition law, empowering the government to forcibly buy land, to include an agricultural tax and enforce a "one-man, one-farm" policy.

"The new act will provide for the agricultural land tax and regulations that pertain to minimum farm sizes, adoption of one-man one-farm concept and the prohibition of ownership of land by foreigners and companies," he said.
The announcement followed a strong message from the government investment promotion agency, saying Zimbabwe was expanding investment areas.

"With Mugabe's plans now, the message reaching potential foreign investors is one of conflicting signals, and its images that matter here," said John Makumbe, a leading Zimbabwean political commentator.
"The world is too busy to read cryptic messages. Very few, and mostly those who understand our politics, will bother," he said.

The state-sponsored Zimbabwe Investment Centre (ZIC) said last week it was trying to lure investors by cutting short to 28 from 60 days the time needed to approve projects and by opening up sectors currently reserved for local investors.

The ZIC law would also be amended to allow new foreign investors to take minority shareholdings in reserved sectors such as food production, primary horticulture, wildlife ranching, livestock development, forestry, fishing and road transportation, with local investors having the controlling stake, it said.
The message was buttressed by Zimbabwe's central bank governor, Leonard Tsumba, who appealed to the government to introduce tax incentives in a July 24 national budget to help attract investors.

Tsumba complained that Zimbabwe -- whose agricultural-driven economy has grown at an average of 1.8 percent annually since 1990 -- had managed to attract only $120 million of about $90 billion of global direct foreign investment in emerging markets in 1995.

Mugabe gave no further details on his new land plans, including what would happen to foreign companies such as Anglo American Corporation and Lonrho who already own vast tracts of land and investments in the southern Africa state.
The companies refused to comment, saying there was insufficient information but one chief executive hinted Mugabe's plans were a "source of worry".

"We are sending unclear if not conflicting signals to foreign investors. We cannot afford to serve messages that are difficult to digest or appear indigestable," said John Robertson, a private economic consultant.
"We already have an image problem with tenders and we cannot afford more problems," he said of controversies that have accompanied the award of government tenders over the past year.
Mugabe's 17-year-old government has been dogged by public accusations that it has been dishing out multi-billion dollar tenders to cronies of top state officials.
The officials, including Mugabe whose nephew Leo Mugabe has won three big tenders in the past few months, deny the charges.

Tsumba told a business seminar that Zimbabwe could help boost its drive for foreign investment by underwriting direct investment inflows, adopting "a transparent, consistent and predictable formal legal and investment code".
